terms.definitionEn: A function expression written with an arrow token and lexical this behavior.
A parameter initializer used when the corresponding argument is omitted or undefined.
A final parameter that gathers remaining arguments into an array.
A syntax that expands iterable values or object properties into another context.
The behavior where an arrow function uses the this value from its surrounding scope.
A returned expression supplied automatically by a concise function body.
The statements or expression executed when a function is called.
A value whose elements can be visited in sequence by iteration syntax.
A new outer collection whose nested object references remain shared with the source.
An individual value collected by the final rest parameter.
A value that can be invoked with function-call syntax.
The named input positions declared for a function.

questions.question: What does this arrow function return for input 4?
questions.explanation: A concise arrow body implicitly returns its expression.

questions.code:
const add = (a, b) => a + b;
console.log(add(2, 5));
questions.explanation: The arrow's expression returns the sum of its parameters.
The omitted argument causes the default parameter value to be used.

questions.prompt: Fill a default value used when the caller provides no title.
questions.explanation: A parameter initializer supplies a value when the argument is omitted.
The parameter pattern takes the first array element.

questions.question: Why are parentheses used before the arrow here?
options: The body must always be an object
They make the result a string
questions.explanation: Empty parentheses represent a parameter list with no parameters.

questions.prompt: Write triple(value) using arrow-function syntax to return three times the input.
questions.explanation: The arrow function has an expression body whose value is returned implicitly.

questions.prompt: Fill the token that separates an arrow function's parameter from its body.
questions.explanation: The arrow token follows the parameter list and precedes the body.

questions.prompt: Write multiplyOrDefault(value, factor), multiplying by factor or by 2 when factor is omitted.
questions.explanation: A default parameter is used when the second argument is omitted.
The first argument fills first, and the remaining two are collected in others.
Spread inserts the existing elements into a new array literal before 3.

questions.prompt: Fill the rest syntax to collect the remaining arguments into values.
questions.explanation: A rest parameter begins with three dots and gathers remaining arguments into an array.

questions.prompt: Write sumAll(...values), returning the sum of any number of numeric arguments.
questions.explanation: The rest parameter collects arguments into an array that can be reduced.

questions.prompt: Fill the syntax to copy every value from source into the new array.
questions.explanation: Spread syntax expands the iterable values into the array literal.

questions.question: Does the default parameter replace the explicitly supplied null?
options: No, null is used because the argument was provided
Yes, null is treated exactly like omission
Yes, every falsy value triggers the default
questions.explanation: Defaults are used for omitted or undefined arguments, not null.

questions.prompt: Write copyAndAppend(values, item), returning a new array with item added without changing values.
questions.explanation: Spread copies the source elements into a new array before appending the item.

questions.question: Does read receive obj as its this value when called as obj.read()?
options: No, arrow functions cannot be called
No, an arrow function uses the surrounding this value
Yes, because value is a property
Yes, every method call binds this to obj
questions.explanation: Arrow functions do not create their own this binding.

questions.code:
function pick(value = 7) { return value; }
console.log(pick(undefined), pick(null));
questions.explanation: undefined activates the default, while null is retained as the supplied argument.

questions.prompt: Fill the syntax to pass every item as a separate function argument.
questions.explanation: Spread expands the array elements into positional arguments.

questions.prompt: Write maxOrNull(...values), returning the largest argument or null when none are provided.
questions.explanation: Check for an empty rest array before expanding it into Math.max.
Object spread is shallow, so both outer values share the nested object.

questions.question: How do rest syntax and spread syntax differ?
keyPoints: Rest gathers multiple values into one array or object
Spread expands values into a surrounding context
Rest appears in parameter or binding positions
Spread can appear in calls and literals
questions.modelAnswer: Rest syntax gathers remaining values into an array or object, such as a function's rest parameter. Spread syntax does the opposite in a context: it expands iterable elements or object properties into a call or literal.

questions.question: When does a default parameter value take effect?
keyPoints: It applies when the argument is omitted
It also applies when the argument is undefined
Defaults are evaluated when the call needs them
questions.modelAnswer: A parameter's default is used when the corresponding argument is omitted or explicitly undefined. Passing null or another value supplies that value instead of activating the default.

questions.question: What are two important differences between arrow functions and regular functions?
keyPoints: Arrow syntax can provide concise expression bodies
They are not constructible with new
Choose regular functions for dynamic this or constructors
questions.modelAnswer: Arrow functions can use concise syntax and take this from their surrounding scope instead of creating their own binding. They also cannot be used as constructors with new, so regular functions remain useful when constructor behavior or dynamic this is needed.
